common_name: Wintergold Dwarf White Fir (Seasonal Gold Flush)

planting.note: Site in full sun in well-drained soil to bring out the strongest spring and fall gold color against the summer green.

directions: 'Wintergold' is a compact white fir selection grown grafted onto Abies firma rootstock, prized for needles that emerge bright chartreuse-yellow in spring, settle to dark green through summer, and flush gold again as cold weather returns. Expect a modest three to four feet of height and two to three feet of width after ten years, making it a slow, dense dwarf fir suited to foundation plantings or conifer collections rather than a quick-growing screen. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil for the strongest seasonal color shift, and expect an eventual mature size well under that of a standard white fir.

common_name: Halgren Momi Fir (Dense Dark-Needled Dwarf)

planting.note: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil; Momi fir cultivars tolerate heat better than most firs, which makes them a good choice for warmer gardens.

directions: 'Halgren' is a selected dwarf form of the Japanese Momi fir, chosen for its dense branching and dark green needle color that holds up well through the growing season. It reaches only five to six feet tall by two to three feet wide after ten years, so it functions as a slow, tidy specimen conifer rather than a forest tree. Abies firma as a species tolerates heat and heavier soils better than many true firs, giving 'Halgren' an advantage in warmer parts of its zone 6-8 range. Give it full sun to light shade and well-drained soil, and expect it to hold a neat, dense silhouette with minimal pruning for many years.

common_name: Faber's Maple (Evergreen Pink-Flushed Maple)

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in sun to part shade, and give young trees winter wind protection toward the colder edge of their range since the foliage is evergreen.

directions: Acer fabri is an uncommon evergreen maple from southern China. Unlike the familiar deciduous maples, it keeps its leathery leaves year-round, with new growth emerging bright pink before maturing to glossy green, giving it ornamental interest beyond typical maple fall color. It wants moist, well-drained soil and does best in sun to part shade, eventually becoming a substantial small tree around 25 feet tall and 20 feet wide. Because evergreen foliage can be damaged by hard freezes, give it a sheltered site and some winter protection near the cold edge of its zone 7-9 range.

common_name: Wako Nishiki Variegated Trident Maple

planting.note: Site in partial shade to protect the pale variegated spring leaves from scorching, moving toward more sun as foliage greens up in summer.

directions: 'Wako Nishiki' is a variegated trident maple selection grown for an unusually dramatic seasonal color sequence: leaves emerge pink, shift to white with green veining, settle into chartreuse green through midsummer, and finish the season in orange and red fall tones. Because the early white-and-pink foliage has reduced chlorophyll, it benefits from some afternoon shade to avoid leaf scorch, with more sun tolerated once leaves green up later in the season. It grows more slowly and typically stays smaller than plain-leaved trident maple seedlings, making it a good specimen for a shaded border or large container.

common_name: Crimson Candles Camellia (Red Reticulata Hybrid)
scientific_name: Camellia reticulata x Camellia fraterna 'Crimson Candles'

planting.note: Plant in full sun for best flowering and densest habit; this hybrid tolerates more sun than most camellias and can be grown as a flowering hedge or screen.

directions: 'Crimson Candles' crosses Camellia reticulata with the more cold-hardy Camellia fraterna, producing an upright, vigorous, densely branched shrub lined with elongated red buds that open into vibrant rose-red to deep pink single flowers two and a half to three inches across. It flowers early, in February and March in North Carolina, well ahead of most azaleas, and performs best with plenty of direct sun, unlike many shade-tolerant camellias. At a projected seven to nine feet tall and five to six feet wide after a decade, it is sized well for use as a flowering screen or informal hedge.

common_name: Ashton's Ballet Camellia (Ballet-Slipper Pink Double)

planting.note: Plant in partial shade with some winter sun protection; this is one of the more cold-hardy fall-blooming camellia hybrids, rated to zone 6a by the breeder.

directions: 'Ashton's Ballet' is a cold-hardy camellia hybrid bred by Dr. William Ackerman in 2000 by crossing Camellia sasanqua 'Shikishima' with Camellia oleifera 'Plain Jane', combining sasanqua-type rose-form double flowers with oleifera's winter toughness. The medium-sized, three- to four-inch blooms open in a soft pink resembling ballet slippers, appearing from October through December in North Carolina. It grows as a vigorous, upright shrub reaching roughly six to seven feet tall and four feet wide after ten years, and its zone 6a hardiness rating makes it plantable well north of where most camellias survive outdoors.

common_name: Elina Cascade Camellia (Weeping Miniature-Flowered)

planting.note: Site where the arching, weeping branches can drape freely, such as above a wall or on a slope, and protect from harsh winter sun and wind at the cold end of its range.

directions: 'Elina Cascade' is a distinctive weeping camellia with arching branches that give it a draping, cascading form rather than the upright habit typical of most camellias. In January and February it covers itself in tiny, miniature pink-lined white flowers that open from drooping pink buds, set against small, purple-tinged leaves. Rated to zone 8 but reported to have survived winters as far north as Atlanta. Its small scale and weeping growth make it well suited to raised beds, retaining walls, or anywhere its arching branches can be seen draping downward, grown in partial shade.

common_name: Duquesa de Coimbra Sasanqua Camellia (Fall-Blooming Pink-Edged)

planting.note: Plant in full sun to partial shade in acidic, well-drained soil; sasanqua camellias tolerate more sun and drier conditions than japonica types, making fall bloom more reliable.

directions: 'Duquesa de Coimbra' is a fall-blooming sasanqua camellia with semi-double flowers in soft pink edged in white, opening as the weather cools in autumn. As a sasanqua, it is more tolerant of sun and drought than the later-blooming japonica camellias, so it can take a more open site while still flowering reliably. Follow standard sasanqua care: acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and protection from harsh winter winds at the colder edge of its range. Use it as a specimen, informal hedge, or espalier where its autumn flower display can be appreciated against the evergreen foliage.

common_name: Betty Ridley Variegated Camellia (White-Blotched Pink Formal Double)

planting.note: Plant in partial shade to protect the virus-variegated foliage and flowers from fading, and give it the sheltered woodland-edge conditions typical camellias prefer.

directions: 'Betty Ridley Variegated' produces medium pink, formal double flowers that are blotched with white, a pattern attributed to a plant virus rather than a stable genetic variegation. This kind of virus-induced color break is prized among camellia collectors for the unpredictable, painterly mottling it adds to otherwise solid-colored flowers. Treat it like other large-flowered camellia cultivars: partial shade, acidic well-drained soil, and protection from harsh winter sun and wind. Because variegated flowers can sometimes revert to solid color on individual branches, occasional pruning of reverted shoots helps maintain the variegated display.

common_name: Gold-Variegated Red-Twig Dogwood (Hedgerows Gold)

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil and cut a third of the oldest canes to the ground each late winter to keep the brightest new red stems coming.

directions: This red-twig dogwood layers gold-and-green variegated leaves over its signature crimson stems, with the variegation blushing pink and red as autumn approaches. It shows its best color in full sun to light shade and in consistently moist to wet soil, making it a strong candidate for rain gardens or stream banks. White spring flower clusters add a secondary point of interest, but the real show is the glowing bare stems through winter once the leaves drop. Renewal-prune the oldest stems yearly rather than shearing the whole plant.

common_name: Superdwarf Olive (Sterile Fruitless Dwarf Olive)

planting.note: Grow in a container with sharp drainage in cold-winter climates so it can be moved under cover, or plant in-ground in zones 8-11 for a tidy, fruitless topiary subject.

directions: Superdwarf olive packs the silvery, elliptic foliage and rugged character of a full-size olive into an ultra-compact shrublet that stays dense without heavy pruning. It flowers lightly in spring but sets no fruit, avoiding the drupe-drop and staining problems of standard olive trees. It wants full, all-day sun and sharply draining soil, and once rooted in is highly drought tolerant. Its small scale and tolerance for shearing make it a natural choice for topiary, formal low hedges, and large containers.

common_name: Calliope Sugar Maple (Pink and White Variegated Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into rich, well-drained soil and site in partial shade, since the streaked white-and-pink leaves can scorch in full afternoon sun.

directions: This chance seedling discovered by breeder Peter Podaras turns the familiar sugar maple into a slow-growing foliage specimen, its leaves splashed irregularly with white and pink through the growing season rather than relying on fall color for interest. Because variegation is a form of reduced chlorophyll, growth is noticeably slower and more compact than a straight-species sugar maple, which makes it workable in smaller landscapes. Give it consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil and afternoon shade protection, and avoid drought stress, which can brown the white leaf sections prematurely.

common_name: Dark Secret Sweetshrub (Maroon-Flowered Hybrid Calycanthus)

planting.note: Set out in spring or fall in loamy, humus-rich soil and allow room for vigorous shoots, since this hybrid grows noticeably fast once established.

directions: Introduced by Broken Arrow Nursery in 2018, this Calycanthus hybrid is a sibling selection to 'Hartlage Wine' but carries several shades darker, near-black maroon flowers with pointed burgundy-red outer tepals surrounding near-white inner petals. The bold, broad leaves can expand to 8-10 inches across on strong new shoots, giving the shrub a coarse, tropical texture that contrasts nicely with fine-leaved neighbors. Grow in full sun to light shade with even moisture for the heaviest late spring to early summer bloom, and prune lightly after flowering to control its vigorous habit.

common_name: Raspberry Rhapsody Fairy Wings (Mahogany-Red Spring Foliage)

planting.note: Tuck divisions or potted starts into shaded woodland soil in spring so roots establish before the first dry summer stretch.

directions: Selected over seven years from an open-pollinated seedling of Epimedium sutchuenense, this 2012 Broken Arrow introduction opens with mahogany-red new leaves that fade to green by midsummer, with mauve-rose spurred flowers and pale pink sepals held just above the foliage mound. Once established, clumps form a tidy, slow-spreading groundcover well suited to dry shade under trees, tolerating root competition better than most woodland perennials. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flower spikes emerge to keep the display clean.

common_name: Space Invaders Fairy Wings (Speckled Long-Spurred Flowers)

planting.note: Plant in rich, well-drained woodland soil in part shade and be patient, since this selection spreads slowly compared to most garden epimediums.

directions: Also a 2012 Broken Arrow Nursery selection from open-pollinated seedlings with Epimedium chlorandrum as the seed parent, this cultivar carries glossy, spiny-edged foliage that stays evergreen and ornamental into January in protected sites. April flowers are distinctive for the group: reflexed white sepals set off pale yellow spurs 1 to 1.5 inches long and flecked with rusty orange speckling, unlike the plainer blooms of most epimediums. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade and avoid soggy conditions, which this slow-spreading selection does not tolerate well.

common_name: Copper Curls Witch Hazel (Burnt-Orange Fall-Blooming Native Shrub)

planting.note: Install as a large multi-stemmed shrub in fall or spring at the edge of woodland light, giving it room to reach 15-20 feet since it eventually behaves like a small understory tree.

directions: Discovered as a chance color-break seedling in a wild Connecticut population and evaluated for over a decade, this is a straight-species common witch hazel selected purely for flower color: ribbon-like, burnt-orange and copper petals that intensify as autumn nights get colder. Because it blooms after leaf drop, the curled, twisted petals show clearly against bare branches, extending the fall color season well past when the foliage itself has gone. As a native Eastern woodland shrub it is easygoing in average garden soil with full sun to part shade, needing only occasional deep watering during its first couple of seasons to establish.

common_name: Sweet Sunshine Witch Hazel (Fragrant Early Spring Yellow Hybrid)

planting.note: Site near a path or entrance where late-winter fragrance can be appreciated, in average well-drained soil with morning sun.

directions: Long grown near Broken Arrow Nursery's own entrance before formal release, this upright hybrid witch hazel was previously circulated informally under a different trial name before being renamed. It produces fragrant, bright yellow flowers in early spring, ahead of most other witch hazel selections, making it a reliable harbinger of the season. Give it full sun to light shade and reasonably fertile, well-drained soil, and prune only to remove crossing branches since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Sunsplash Winterberry Holly (Gold-Splashed Variegated Foliage)

planting.note: Plant alongside a male pollinator such as 'Jim Dandy' since this female selection needs a nearby mate to set its orange-red fruit.

directions: Discovered by John Dancher, this is a rare variegated sport of the native deciduous winterberry holly, carrying bright gold-splashed leaves through the growing season in addition to the orange-red berries the species is known for. It needs a compatible male winterberry such as 'Jim Dandy' planted nearby to pollinate its flowers, since hollies are dioecious and this is a female clone. Like its wild parent it is naturally adapted to moist-to-wet soils, so it performs best in full sun with consistent moisture, including boggy or streamside sites that most shrubs cannot tolerate.

common_name: Hammonasset Sheep Laurel (Blush-Rose Native Connecticut Selection)

planting.note: Plant in acidic, consistently moist, well-drained soil mimicking boggy native habitat, in sun to light shade.

directions: Selected by Broken Arrow founder Richard Jaynes from a wild stand of sheep laurel growing near Hammonasset in Madison, Connecticut, this clone was chosen for producing unusually consistent, high-quality flower displays compared to typical wild seedlings. It carries clusters of rich blush-rose flowers on a small, broadleaf evergreen shrub considerably smaller than its relative mountain laurel, making it useful for tight native plantings or bog-garden edges. Give it acidic, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist, since sheep laurel naturally occurs in damp, peaty sites across its native range.

common_name: Fire and Ice Tatarian Dogwood (White-Edged Foliage, Scarlet Winter Stems)

planting.note: Plant in full sun for the brightest winter stem color, in average to consistently moist soil, and renew a third of the oldest stems each spring to keep colorful new wood coming.

directions: Found as a chance branch mutation on Cornus alba 'Cardinal' and introduced by Broken Arrow in 2018, this multi-stemmed dogwood runs through three distinct seasonal looks: foliage that opens near-white in spring, settles to fresh green by summer, and turns orange-red in fall, followed by vivid orange-scarlet bark once the leaves drop. Because the colorful stems are the main winter feature, plant it where bare branches will be visible against snow or a dark backdrop. Keep soil evenly moist to average and cut the oldest canes to the ground every year or two, since the brightest stem color comes from vigorous young growth.

common_name: Gilded Daybreak Holly (Golden-Yellow Evergreen Foliage, Scarlet Berries)

planting.note: Site with a bit of afternoon shade to prevent winter leaf burn, in average garden soil, and plant a male blue holly nearby to ensure fruit set.

directions: Found as a branch mutation on the hybrid blue holly 'Honey Jo' and introduced by Broken Arrow in 2018, this selection replaces the typical blue-green meserveae leaf color with rich golden-yellow foliage that turns especially vivid in autumn against scarlet-orange berries. It builds a dense branch framework at a moderate pace, adding roughly 3-5 inches of new growth per year, so it fills in as a tidy foundation or hedge shrub without becoming unruly quickly. As with other blue hollies it is female and needs a compatible male pollinator nearby, and benefits from a touch of afternoon shade to keep the gold foliage from bleaching in strong summer sun.
